name: Faro
brief: One runway, one arrival stream, and the sea on three sides. Traffic comes down the coast from the north-west or in off the Atlantic from the south, and there is nothing in the way of either: no high ground, no neighbouring field to work around, and room to take an aircraft out over the Gulf of Cadiz and bring it back if the sequence goes wrong. The single runway is the whole constraint -- everything lands on the same strip of tarmac, so the job is spacing rather than sorting. The gentlest place to learn what a vector does.

Mediterranean traffic routing west out over the Atlantic

provenance.notes: The aerodrome reference point, the runway designators and bearings, and the field elevation are real to the best of the author knowledge. EVERYTHING ELSE IS CONSTRUCTED: the entry fixes and their names, the airspace boundary, the terrain and noise areas and the traffic mix are invented to give the sector a shape to control, and are NOT taken from any AIP. Do not use for anything but this game. Contrast egll.json, whose positions are surveyed. Runway thresholds are derived from the strip: a centre on the reference point, the published bearing, and the published length, with the two ends half a length either side. Only the aerodrome VOR carries a frequency; the entry gates are plain waypoints. The airspace volumes are CONSTRUCTED and are not from any AIP or sector file: a control zone shaped round the runway, approach corridors on the extended centrelines, and terminal sectors whose floors step up away from the arrival direction and over the high ground in this file. They carry derivation "approx". Aerodrome traffic zones are computed from a rule -- 2.5 NM where the longest runway is over 1850 m and 2 NM otherwise, to 2000 ft above the aerodrome -- and carry derivation "rule". The control zone and the terminal area outline are unchanged and still rule-derived. Everything else in the airspace block is CONSTRUCTED and comes from no AIP or sector file: approach corridors along the extended centrelines, which bring the base of controlled airspace down to 1500 ft outside the zone, and terminal sub-areas whose bases step up away from the arrival direction and over the high ground in this file. They carry derivation "approx". None of them encloses the aerodrome, so none of them joins the area of responsibility: that is still the control zone and the terminal area, exactly as before. Aerodrome traffic zones are computed from a rule -- 2.5 NM where the longest runway is over 1850 m and 2 NM otherwise, to 2000 ft above the aerodrome -- and carry derivation "rule".
